text: Praise the LORD! Praise the LORD, O my soul!
I will praise the LORD as long as I live; I will sing praise to my God as long as I have breath.

versions.text: I will praise the LORD as long as I live; I will sing to my God while I have my being.
versions.explanation: "While I have my being" is archaic and stumbles when read aloud. The Hebrew בְּעוֹדִי simply means "while I still exist / as long as I am," and a more natural parallel to the first line reads better orally.

text: Do not put your trust in princes, in mortals, who cannot save.
When their breath departs, they return to the dust; on that day all their plans come to nothing.

versions.text: When their breath departs, they return to the earth; on that day their plans come to nothing.
versions.explanation: אַדְמָתוֹ refers to the ground/soil from which humanity was formed; "the dust" conveys the mortality imagery more clearly than the ambiguous "the earth," which can be read as the planet.

text: Blessed is the one whose help is the God of Jacob, whose hope is in the LORD his God—
the Maker of heaven and earth, of the sea and everything in them, who keeps faith forever;
who brings justice to the oppressed and gives bread to the hungry. The LORD sets the prisoners free.
The LORD opens the eyes of the blind; the LORD lifts up those who are bowed down; the LORD loves the righteous.
The LORD watches over the stranger; he sustains the orphan and the widow, but the way of the wicked he brings to ruin.
The LORD reigns forever—your God, O Zion, from generation to generation. Praise the LORD!

versions.text: The LORD reigns forever, your God, O Zion, through all generations. Praise the LORD!
versions.explanation: The stacked appositions read awkwardly aloud; a dash marks the break clearly, and "from generation to generation" better reflects the repeated לְדֹר וָדֹר while keeping the closing rhythm.
